objection: Does ‘firstborn of creation’ mean Jesus was created?
answer:
This is a fair challenge, and you're right that "firstborn" ordinarily implies membership in the group being born — that's exactly the point I'd concede if Paul had stopped at Colossians 1:15. But he didn't. The very next verse tells us what he means by the title: "for by him were all things created" (Colossians 1:16). Paul is his own best interpreter here, and he explicitly places Christ outside the class of "all things" as its Maker rather than inside it as one of its members. To say the firstborn of all creation is also the creator of all creation would be flatly incoherent if "firstborn" meant "first thing made" — you can't create the category you're a member of, in its entirety, without creating yourself.

That's why the passages point instead to the biblical sense of "firstborn" as a title of rank and inheritance rather than birth-sequence — Psalm 89:27 calls David God's "firstborn" though he was neither God's first nor only son; the word marks him as preeminent heir, not literally begotten first. Applied to Christ, "firstborn of all creation" means He holds the位 of supremacy and inheritance over creation — precisely because, as verse 16 says, all things were created "by him, and for him."

As for your direct question — I can't point you to a case where "firstborn among X" definitely excludes the person from X by usage alone; that's not where the argument rests. It rests on Paul's own explanatory clause. The context, not a general rule about the word, settles the sense here — and Colossians 1:16-17 places Christ unambiguously on the Creator's side of the line, "before all things," holding all things together, which no creature could be said to do.

transcript.content:
# A Unitarian's Challenge on "Firstborn of Creation"

Look at Colossians 1:15 directly — "the firstborn of all creation." In every natural use of language, "firstborn" means the first one *born*, the eldest in a series. If I say someone is the "firstborn of my children," nobody supposes they were never born. So when Paul calls Jesus the *firstborn of all creation*, the most straightforward reading is that he ranks first *among* created things — he's the supreme creature, not the uncreated Creator. Your argument that "firstborn" doesn't mean "created" requires you to read past the plain sense of the words. Can you show me another passage where "firstborn of" or "firstborn among" a group means the person *isn't actually part* of that group?

This is a fair challenge, and you're right that "firstborn" ordinarily implies membership in the group being born — that's exactly the point I'd concede if Paul had stopped at Colossians 1:15. But he didn't. The very next verse tells us what he means by the title: "for by him were all things created" (Colossians 1:16). Paul is his own best interpreter here, and he explicitly places Christ outside the class of "all things" as its Maker rather than inside it as one of its members. To say the firstborn of all creation is also the creator of all creation would be flatly incoherent if "firstborn" meant "first thing made" — you can't create the category you're a member of, in its entirety, without creating yourself.

That's why the passages point instead to the biblical sense of "firstborn" as a title of rank and inheritance rather than birth-sequence — Psalm 89:27 calls David God's "firstborn" though he was neither God's first nor only son; the word marks him as preeminent heir, not literally begotten first. Applied to Christ, "firstborn of all creation" means He holds the位 of supremacy and inheritance over creation — precisely because, as verse 16 says, all things were created "by him, and for him."

As for your direct question — I can't point you to a case where "firstborn among X" definitely excludes the person from X by usage alone; that's not where the argument rests. It rests on Paul's own explanatory clause. The context, not a general rule about the word, settles the sense here — and Colossians 1:16-17 places Christ unambiguously on the Creator's side of the line, "before all things," holding all things together, which no creature could be said to do.
